title: Filtering Data: WHERE, Operators & Pattern Matching — Narration Scripts

lecture.New_Day3Part1audio01.mp3: The WHERE clause is the core row-level filter in SQL. The database evaluates the boolean condition in WHERE for every candidate row coming from the FROM clause. Only rows where the condition evaluates to TRUE pass through — any row evaluating to FALSE or NULL is filtered out.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio02.mp3: Here is the minimal WHERE clause structure. First, write SELECT followed by your desired columns. Next, write FROM followed by the table name. Finally, write WHERE followed by your filtering condition — for example, WHERE salary is greater than eighty thousand.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio03.mp3: Execution order is crucial: in SQL, WHERE runs as Step 2 — right after FROM, but before GROUP BY, HAVING, and SELECT. This means WHERE cannot reference column aliases defined in the SELECT list, because those aliases do not exist yet at filtering time.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio04.mp3: SQL provides six core comparison operators to build WHERE conditions. Let's explore each one.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio05.mp3: The equals operator checks for an exact match. The not equal operator, written as less-than greater-than or exclamation-equals, tests for inequality. The greater than and less than operators test numerical and date boundaries. The greater than or equal, and less than or equal operators include the boundary value itself in your results.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio06.mp3: Here are comparison operators in action. The first query retrieves employees with a salary exceeding sixty thousand using greater than. The second finds products where stock quantity is zero or less using less than or equal. The third uses the not equal operator to filter out a specific department.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio07.mp3: When you need to combine multiple conditions, SQL provides three fundamental logical operators: NOT, AND, and OR.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio08.mp3: The NOT operator inverts a condition: NOT TRUE becomes FALSE, and NOT FALSE becomes TRUE. Use it to cleanly exclude specific values or negate complex filters.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio09.mp3: The AND operator returns TRUE only when both conditions are met at the same time. If even one condition is FALSE, the entire AND filter evaluates to FALSE.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio10.mp3: The OR operator returns TRUE as long as at least one condition is met. Both conditions must be FALSE for the OR filter to fail.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio11.mp3: Operator precedence dictates the evaluation order: NOT evaluates first, followed by AND, and then OR. Because AND binds before OR, always use parentheses when combining AND with OR to make your logic crystal clear and prevent subtle bugs.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio12.mp3: Here are logical operators in practice. The first query uses the AND operator to find active employees in department twenty. The second uses the OR operator to find customers in the North or South region. The third uses the NOT operator with LIKE to exclude a specific name pattern.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio13.mp3: Here is a critical trap: whenever NULL is involved in any comparison, the result is UNKNOWN — not TRUE and not FALSE. Because WHERE strictly requires a TRUE result to include a row, rows comparing against NULL are discarded. Always use the is null or is not null predicates to explicitly test for missing values.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio14.mp3: Next is the BETWEEN operator. BETWEEN low AND high is a clean shorthand for writing greater than or equal to low, and less than or equal to high. Both endpoints are strictly inclusive, and it works seamlessly on numbers, dates, and text.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio15.mp3: Here are BETWEEN examples in action. The first query filters employees earning between fifty thousand and ninety thousand using the BETWEEN operator. The second retrieves all orders placed in twenty twenty-four using date boundaries. And the third uses the NOT BETWEEN operator to cleanly select products outside a given price band.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio16.mp3: When using the BETWEEN operator, always place the smaller value first, such as BETWEEN fifty AND one hundred. Writing BETWEEN one hundred AND fifty will return zero rows — it is syntactically valid SQL, but logically empty.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio17.mp3: Here is a major date precision gotcha: specifying a date range with the BETWEEN operator truncates the end date to midnight. Any transactions occurring later in the day on December thirty-first will be completely missed. A much safer industry pattern is using greater than or equal to the start date and strictly less than the start of next year.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio18.mp3: Next is the in operator. The in operator is a concise replacement for chaining multiple OR conditions. The database engine checks whether a column's value matches any item in the provided list. The not in operator inverts the check, returning only rows absent from the list.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio19.mp3: Here are in operator examples. The first query checks if department ID is in ten, twenty, or thirty using the in operator. The second finds customers located in North, South, or East regions. And the third uses the not in operator to exclude specific department IDs.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio20.mp3: Beware of this dangerous trap: if the list passed to the not in operator contains even a single null value, the entire query returns zero rows. Because comparisons against null yield UNKNOWN, the entire AND chain becomes UNKNOWN. When working with subqueries, always filter out nulls with the is not null predicate or use NOT EXISTS.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio21.mp3: Now let's explore the LIKE operator for pattern matching with wildcards. The LIKE operator performs partial text searches, such as finding all customer names starting with a letter or email addresses from a specific domain.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio22.mp3: The percent wildcard matches any sequence of zero or more characters in the LIKE operator. R percent matches names starting with R. Percent A matches names ending with A. Percent ESH percent finds the substring anywhere. And percent at gmail dot com filters emails from Gmail.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio23.mp3: The underscore wildcard matches exactly one single character in the LIKE operator. R followed by four underscores matches exactly five-letter names starting with R. Three underscores matches three-character product codes. And combining them, like underscore OO percent, matches any string where the second and third characters are OO.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio24.mp3: Here are complete queries using the LIKE operator. The first retrieves employees whose first name begins with S. The second finds products containing the word Mouse. And the third uses the NOT LIKE operator to exclude all Gmail addresses.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio25.mp3: Keep in mind that case sensitivity for the LIKE operator depends on your database engine. In SQLite and MySQL, LIKE is case-insensitive by default for ASCII text. In PostgreSQL, LIKE is case-sensitive, so use the ILIKE operator for case-insensitive matching. In SQL Server, behavior depends on the column's collation.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio26.mp3: Next is handling missing data with the is null and is not null predicates. In SQL, null represents a missing, unknown, or inapplicable value. The fundamental rule: you cannot test for null with the equals operator. Always use the is null or is not null predicates.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio27.mp3: Here are is null examples in practice. The first finds top-level employees who have no manager using the is null predicate. The second finds employees who report to a manager using the is not null predicate. The third finds staff with no commission using is null. And the fourth retrieves active employees who do earn a commission using is not null.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio28.mp3: Never write WHERE commission equals null or not equal to null. Both comparisons produce UNKNOWN and silently discard every row. The is null predicate is the dedicated SQL operator built specifically to detect missing values.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio29.mp3: Now for our first interview question: why does WHERE commission equals null return no rows even when employees have null commission? Because in SQL, null represents an unknown value. Any comparison against null evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE. Because WHERE only retains rows that evaluate to TRUE, UNKNOWN rows are discarded. You must use the is null predicate.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio30.mp3: Second interview question: why does WHERE department ID not in return zero rows when the subquery has a null? Because SQL internally expands the not in operator into a chain of NOT EQUAL comparisons. Comparing against null yields UNKNOWN, which breaks the entire AND chain. The fix is adding WHERE department ID is not null to the subquery or rewriting with NOT EXISTS.
lecture.New_Day3Part1audio31.mp3: Third interview question: what is the performance impact of leading wildcards with the LIKE operator, such as WHERE name LIKE percent Manager percent? A leading percent wildcard forces a full table scan because the B-tree index cannot be used. For large datasets, use a Full-Text Search index, or anchor the pattern to the start of the string.

questions.New_Day3Question01.mp3: Ready to filter by price? Retrieve the name and unit price of all products with a price greater than ten thousand. Sort the results by unit price descending.
questions.New_Day3Question01sol.mp3: Let's write this query. SELECT name, unit price... FROM products... WHERE unit price is greater than ten thousand... ORDER BY unit price DESC. The WHERE clause filters out all products at or below ten thousand, and ORDER BY arranges the remaining products from most expensive to least.
questions.New_Day3Question02.mp3: Time to filter by region! Retrieve first name, last name, and region for customers in either the North or East region. Use the in operator.
questions.New_Day3Question02sol.mp3: Here is the solution. SELECT first name, last name, and region... FROM customers... WHERE region in North comma East. The in operator is a clean alternative to chaining multiple OR conditions — it checks whether the region matches any value in your list.
questions.New_Day3Question03.mp3: Let's practice the BETWEEN operator! Find employees earning between sixty thousand and one hundred thousand inclusive. Retrieve first name, last name, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question03sol.mp3: Let's code this. SELECT first name, last name, and salary... FROM employees... WHERE salary BETWEEN sixty thousand AND one hundred thousand. The BETWEEN operator is inclusive on both boundaries — it is equivalent to writing salary greater than or equal to sixty thousand AND salary less than or equal to one hundred thousand.
questions.New_Day3Question04.mp3: Time to search with pattern matching! Find all employees whose first name starts with the letter S. Retrieve first name, last name, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question04sol.mp3: The solution uses the LIKE operator. SELECT first name, last name, and salary... FROM employees... WHERE first name LIKE quote S percent quote. The percent wildcard matches any sequence of characters — so S percent matches any name starting with S followed by any number of characters.
questions.New_Day3Question05.mp3: Let's combine two conditions with the AND operator! Find active employees — where is active equals one — who are in department twenty. Retrieve first name, department ID, and salary.
questions.New_Day3Question05sol.mp3: Here is the query. SELECT first name, department ID, and salary... FROM employees... WHERE is active equals one AND department ID equals twenty. Both conditions must evaluate to TRUE for a row to pass. The AND operator is the exact operator needed here because we want employees who are simultaneously active AND in department twenty.
questions.New_Day3Question06.mp3: Final challenge — NULL handling! Find all employees who have no commission assigned. Retrieve first name, last name, and commission.
questions.New_Day3Question06sol.mp3: The solution uses the is null predicate. SELECT first name, last name, and commission... FROM employees... WHERE commission is null. Critical rule: you cannot write commission equals null — that always produces UNKNOWN and discards every row. The is null predicate is the only correct way to test for missing data in SQL.
